extracted.intended_audience: health and medical journalists (reporters/editors covering studies, conferences, and peer-reviewed research)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for journalists on how to handle, evaluate, and respond to embargoed scientific and medical releases (including recognizing problematic embargo practices and options when embargoes are restrictive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize how embargoed material is distributed
rubrics_metrics.description: Many journals and scientific societies release material to reporters on an embargoed basis, often using a service such as Eurekalert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the channels (e.g., Eurekalert) and typical practices so you can anticipate what will be released and when; being on distribution lists is how many outlets get simultaneous access to studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand consequences of breaking embargoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists who publish stories before those embargoes lift can be punished by losing access to future materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat embargoes as having real access consequences — consider trade-offs before publishing early, because you may be blocked from future press materials from that journal or society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of the Ingelfinger Rule and its effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ingelfinger Rule (originating at NEJM) says the journal will reject papers if their findings had been reported by the media first, which can stymie reporters' attempts to cover unpublished research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with unpublished research, check whether the target journal enforces an Ingelfinger-type policy; that may limit what you can report without jeopardizing publication of the research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question whether embargoes improve journalism or make it lazy
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargoes can punctuate the scientific process with 'news events,' but critics argue they make journalists lazy, chasing 'journal hits' instead of doing original, enterprising reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the big picture before agreeing to an embargo — avoid letting embargo schedules drive your news judgment or discourage more original reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for inconsistent or problematic embargo practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals and societies all deal with embargoes differently: some refuse to lift embargoes after early reports; others insist on 'ridiculously short embargoes'; some embargo materials that are already published; some set an embargo that lifts at a reporter's local time (giving geographic advantage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to these red flags (refusing to lift embargoes, extremely short windows, embargoing already-published material, local-time lifting) and factor them into whether to accept or push back on an embargo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question stated purpose of embargoes
rubrics_metrics.description: If journals insist on very short embargoes or embargo material already public, it calls into question whether their policy is truly 'to help journalists' or instead to control information flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically evaluate whether an embargo seems designed to inform journalists or to control publicity; challenge policies that appear to serve the latter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remember the mantra: 'You can't embargo something that is already in the public domain.'
rubrics_metrics.description: If material is already public, the embargo claim has no force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether content has already been released; use that fact when negotiating or challenging an embargo with the issuing institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate or discuss problematic embargoes with the issuing institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes it works to just discuss the policy with the embargoing institution and get them to change it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an embargo seems unfair or restrictive, raise the issue with the institution/publisher — some policies have been changed after journalists questioned them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use investigative pressure when negotiation fails (turn the tables)
rubrics_metrics.description: If discussion doesn't work, perform digging or reporting on the policy itself (example: USA Today's Steve Sternberg turned the tables after investigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly exposing or questioning a restrictive policy can lead societies or journals to revise it; consider investigative approaches as a lever for change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know which journals are consistent or inconsistent in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outlets (e.g., JAMA and the Archives journals; Nature) are relatively consistent about embargo handling, while others vary widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track journal-specific practices over time so you know which organizations are likely to be reasonable and which are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage professional networks and advocacy groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations and individuals (e.g., Embargo Watch, Retraction Watch, Association of Health Care Journalists, knowledgeable editors like Ivan Oransky) can help push back on restrictive policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you encounter problematic embargoes, share examples with professional groups, ask for advice, or publicize the issue; two societies changed policies after the author wrote about them, and AHCJ is collecting examples.
